6.text: There are several other methods of divination; for instance, the person

7.text: puts an amulet or a splinter of wood into his left mitten, and shakes it

8.text: violently till the small object flies out of the mitten. It is a good sign if it

9.text: falls to the right: the contrary is a bad sign. Divination with blades of grass

10.text: is very common. The person takes eight blades of grass, and, forming a

11.text: slender sheaf, ties it in the middle; then he ties consecutively the ends of

12.text: the grass-blades which touch one another, after which the sheaf is undone.

13.text: If the blades were so tied as to form an uninterrupted circle, the indication

14.text: is favorable: if not, it is unfavorable. Such a method seems almost sure to

15.text: prognosticate bad luck. Many persons, however, succeeded in my presence in

16.text: forming a circle of blades tied together. I cannot tell whether this was the

17.text: result of good luck or of cleverness, though they assured me that the thing was

18.text: done quite honestly without any trick. In a former chapter² I alluded to the
18.note: footnote marker: machine draft read '?'; raster shows superscript 2, anchoring footnote 2 (line 44).

19.text: use, among the Maritime Chukchee, of lumps of tallow for purposes of divination.

20.text: Dreams. — I have already spoken of the influence of dreams in the

21.text: arrangement of the various details of Chukchee ceremonials.³ In arranging

22.text: the thanksgiving ceremonial and the races, dreams are especially important.

31.text: Once when I was travelling with a party of Chukchee in the country of

32.text: the Dry Anui, we stopped over night on the shores of a certain lake. In

33.text: the morning one of the natives told us that the owner of the lake came to

34.text: him in a dream and asked him for a sacrifice. “You are a new-comer to this

35.text: country,” said the owner of the lake. “You must give me a present.” The

36.text: man was actually a new-comer to that part of the country. Accordingly he

37.text: sacrificed to the lake a piece of tobacco-leaf and a small lump of sugar.

38.text: But the “spirit” had in mind some other thing. The native had with him a

39.text: little brandy in a glass bottle, which he was carrying as a present to his old
